name: Concrete cylinder
seoTitle: Concrete cylinder Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Concrete cylinder: work out diameter from the height and the weight. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Concrete cylinder calculator the height, the weight, the bag size and the cost of each bag of pre-mix concrete and it returns diameter. It is built for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Concrete cylinder calculator work?
sections.html:
The Concrete cylinder calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports diameter in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the concerete mix and the concrete mix ratio); then you type in the height, the weight, the bag size and the cost of each bag of pre-mix concrete.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Concrete cylinder calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Diameter=2 × the square root of (volume ÷ (height × quantity)) ÷ the square root of (PI)
Concrete density=weight ÷ volume
Waste=100 × bag size × bags needed ÷ weight − 100
Bags needed=total cost ÷ cost of each bag of pre-mix concrete
Volume=total cost ÷ cost of concrete per unit volume
Cost per column=total cost ÷ quantity

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Volume, opening in cubic centimeters
  • %, opening in percent
  • Volume, opening in cubic centimeters
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Mass, opening in kilograms

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Concrete cylinder calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the height, the weight and the bag size — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Concrete cylinder calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns diameter, derived from the height, the weight and the bag size. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Concrete cylinder calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the height, the weight, the bag size and the cost of each bag of pre-mix concrete, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter diameter in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Diameter opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Concrete cylinder calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
